clue.text: Pay Bill to give Greek character a lift close to pub

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only its final letter is wanted

blocks.note: to give someone a lift in a car is to pick them up
theta is the eighth letter of the Greek alphabet
the final letter of pub

explanation.surface: Someone settling up a bill in a bar after giving a Greek friend a ride to the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'give Greek character a lift' as PICK UP THETA, then add the end of pub; 'Pay Bill' looks like a person's name but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To pick up the tab is an idiom for paying the bill for everyone, as at a restaurant.

clue.text: Case is conspicuous when going around island

indicators.note: going around something means wrapping it, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: patent means plain or obvious
I is the standard abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: A detective case that becomes obvious once someone travels round an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' suggests a detective story, but here it is a medical case: a person under treatment.
explanation.definitionFit: Doctors refer to a person under their care as a case, so a case can be a hospital patient.

clue.text: Courses cooked for wealthy king

indicators.note: cooking changes raw ingredients into something new, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A banquet of courses prepared for a rich monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Croesus was a king of Lydia famed for his riches, as in the phrase 'rich as Croesus'.

clue.text: European articles deteriorate in drawers, perhaps

blocks.note: UN is a French article and DER a German one
to wear is to become worn or degraded through use

explanation.surface: Items of European clothing going off in a chest of drawers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawers' suggests furniture, but here it means knickers, an example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Drawers is an old word for knickers or underpants, so they are one kind of the garments named.

clue.text: Rhythm in work by The Police rising

indicators.note: in a down entry, something rising is read from the bottom up, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: OP is short for opus, a work
the Met is London's Metropolitan Police

explanation.surface: Discussing the beat in a song by the band The Police climbing the charts.
explanation.walkthrough: The Police were a rock band, but here they are London's police force.
explanation.definitionFit: Tempo is the speed or pace of a piece of music, its beat or rhythm.

clue.text: Periodically, we're slyly held up by US president, elusive and slippery

indicators.note: something done periodically happens at regular intervals, so every other letter is taken

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters
Ike was the nickname of President Dwight Eisenhower

explanation.surface: A sly character, mocked as slippery, being delayed by an American president.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry, 'held up by' places the first part on top of the second.
explanation.definitionFit: An eel is notoriously hard to grasp, so eel-like describes someone evasive and slippery.

clue.text: In danger, only 50 per cent of cheats cheat

indicators.note: fifty per cent is half, so only half of the following word's letters are kept

blocks.note: the back half of this word
to take someone in is to cheat them

explanation.surface: A grumble that a gambling den is risky because half the players are cheating.
explanation.definitionFit: Something at stake is liable to be lost, so it is in jeopardy.

clue.text: Solver rapidly worked out Jack Straw's former role

indicators.note: something worked out has been processed and rearranged, so these letters are reordered

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: The solver quickly deduces which government post a politician once held.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack Straw is a Labour politician who served in the British cabinet under Tony Blair.
explanation.definitionFit: Straw held the ceremonial cabinet office of Lord Privy Seal in 2006-07, alongside leading the House of Commons.

clue.text: Youngster bound to be supported by Coward

blocks.note: to bound is to leap or spring
a chicken is slang for a coward

explanation.surface: A young person destined to be backed by Noel Coward, the playwright.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital C makes Coward look like the dramatist Noel Coward; in a down entry, 'supported by' puts the coward underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: A spring chicken is an idiom for a young person, usually in 'no spring chicken'.

clue.text: Audibly blooming vulgar

blocks.note: flowers in bloom are said to be out
loud can mean garish or vulgar, as of clothes

explanation.surface: Someone audibly swearing, with 'blooming' as a mild vulgar oath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blooming' reads as a mild British expletive, but here it means flowering.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying something out loud means speaking it so that it can be heard, the sense of audibly.

clue.text: Namby-pamby lawyer and cleaner swapping starters

indicators.note: two words exchanging their starters trade their first letters with each other

blocks.note: a silk is a senior barrister, a King's Counsel, who wears a silk gown
a mop is a floor-cleaning tool

explanation.surface: A wet lawyer and an office cleaner trading jobs.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the opening letters of the two words so S and M change places.
explanation.definitionFit: Namby-pamby used as a noun means a feeble, weak person, and milksop is a synonym for such a weakling.

clue.text: Theatre worker's shift possibly next to emergency room

blocks.note: a shift is a simple straight dress, so one example
ER is the abbreviation for emergency room

explanation.surface: A stagehand's work shift could be spent beside a hospital's emergency room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shift' reads as a period of work, but it is a garment.
explanation.definitionFit: A dresser in a theatre helps actors into and out of their costumes backstage.

clue.text: Business that's turning over, or folding?

definitions.text: Business that's turning over, or folding?

blocks.clueFragment: Business that's turning over, or folding?
blocks.note: surface reading: a company either with a healthy turnover or about to go bust

blocks.clueFragment: Business that's turning over, or folding?
blocks.note: setter's reading: a pastime that consists of turning paper over and creasing it into shapes

explanation.walkthrough: Turnover and folding are both business words for trading and failing; here they describe what the hands do to a sheet of paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Origami is the Japanese art of making models by creasing and turning a square of paper.

clue.text: Registers rested soldiers coming back

indicators.note: coming back means returning the way it came, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: to have sat is to have taken a rest
OR stands for Other Ranks, ordinary soldiers

explanation.surface: Duty lists record which troops have had a rest on their return.
explanation.definitionFit: A rota is a register or roster showing who is on duty when.

clue.text: Get Grease hit as DVD's hidden feature?

indicators.note: something hit is knocked about and battered, so these letters are shaken into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Buy the hit film musical Grease on disc and find a bonus extra.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hit' sits naturally after Grease, the 1978 hit musical, but it is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: An Easter egg is a secret extra hidden in software or on a disc, named after eggs hidden for children to find.

clue.text: Something tasty from The Gap – it's new

indicators.note: making something new means changing its form, so these letters are put in a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: An item bought from the clothing store Gap, announced as a new arrival.
explanation.definitionFit: Spaghetti is a popular pasta, an example of a tasty food; the definition is deliberately vague.

clue.text: Conversely, Gripper Stebson initially interrupting Lynn?

indicators.note: initially points to the start of the name, so only its opening letter is used
to interrupt is to break into the middle of something, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: a vice is a tool that grips work in place
Vera Lynn was the British wartime singer known as the Forces' Sweetheart
the first letter of the name

explanation.surface: A bully from children's TV butting in on the singer Vera Lynn.
explanation.walkthrough: Gripper Stebson was the school bully in the British children's drama Grange Hill; the name splits so that Gripper is a tool and Stebson gives one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Vice versa is a Latin phrase meaning the other way round, so conversely.

clue.text: Bread produced by man at one

blocks.note: a chap is a man
taken as written
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A loaf baked by a lone man.
explanation.definitionFit: A chapati is a flat unleavened bread from South Asian cooking.

clue.text: Virginia shown up, very tired as usual

indicators.note: in a down entry, something shown up is read from the bottom upwards, so its letters run backwards

blocks.note: VA is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Virginia
all in is an idiom for exhausted

explanation.surface: A visitor from Virginia turns up, exhausted as always.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shown up' looks attached to Virginia, but it reverses the phrase after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Vanilla is slang for plain or ordinary, the standard version without extras, so usual.

clue.text: Tense argument about hotel price

indicators.note: about can mean turned round, so the words before it are read backwards

blocks.note: T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense
a row is a quarrel
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A heated dispute over what a hotel room costs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like it means concerning, but it turns round the two words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Worth is the value of something, the amount it would fetch, so its price.

clue.text: Sang sweetly – and brawled unexpectedly

indicators.note: something that happens unexpectedly is out of the expected order, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A singer who performed beautifully then got into a fight out of nowhere.
explanation.definitionFit: To warble is to sing with trills like a songbird, in a sweet melodic way.

clue.text: Partly upset apple-cart, ardently struggling to get ahead?

indicators.note: partly means only part of the following words is used, a run of letters inside them
upset means turned over, so in this down entry the run of letters is read backwards

blocks.note: the run spanning the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Someone eagerly upsetting the apple-cart in order to get on in life.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a phrase describing the answer, with a question mark because it is a description rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: The rat race is the fierce competitive struggle of working life, everyone scrambling to get ahead.

clue.text: Stop aunt cycling in school

indicators.note: cycling means going round in a loop, so letters move from one end of the word to the other
in places the first piece inside the second

blocks.note: taken as written
SCH is the abbreviation for school

explanation.walkthrough: Move the last letter of aunt to the front to get the cycled form.
explanation.definitionFit: To staunch is to stop a flow, especially of blood from a wound.

clue.text: Monster's heads you don't relish attacking, first of all

indicators.note: first of all asks for the first letter of every word in the phrase

blocks.note: the initial letters of these five words

explanation.surface: A beast whose many heads nobody would enjoy taking on.
explanation.walkthrough: Fittingly, the hydra of Greek myth had many heads, which grew back when cut off.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hydra was the many-headed serpent killed by Hercules, so a mythical monster.

clue.text: Dissenter's quote on closure of church retracted

indicators.note: the closure of a word is where it finishes, so only its final letter is taken

blocks.note: to cite is to quote
re means on or about, as in a letter heading
the last letter of church

explanation.surface: A rebel's statement about a church shutting down is withdrawn.
explanation.definitionFit: A heretic holds views at odds with accepted doctrine, so is a dissenter from orthodoxy.

clue.text: Was of help to five in car club – one steered

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

blocks.note: the AA is the Automobile Association, a British motoring organisation

I is the Roman numeral for one
to have led is to have guided or steered

clue.text: Ploughing up to date?

explanation.walkthrough: 'Up to date' reads as one phrase meaning current, but it splits into two parts.
explanation.definitionFit: Tillage is the cultivation of land by ploughing and harrowing it.

clue.text: Appropriate when American con is in good nick

blocks.note: fit means suitable or appropriate
as can mean when, as in 'as he left'
A is a standard abbreviation for American
a fiddle is a swindle

explanation.surface: An American fraudster is suitably jailed, nick being slang for prison.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' is British slang both for prison and for condition, as in good nick meaning in good shape.
explanation.definitionFit: Fit as a fiddle is an idiom for being in excellent health, the same as in good condition.
